chapter: Decca, Cow Cow Blues and royalties
title: Cow Cow Blues leads to Decca work with Peetie Wheatstraw and others
summary: Cow Cow vouches for him to Mayo Williams; Price then accompanies Peetie Wheatstraw, Little Brother Montgomery and others, and Bob Crosby borrows his arrangement.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Right. "Sam Price and His Four Quarters." And Mayo liked me. But I didn't see him any more until I saw him in Chicago years later. And when I saw him in Chicago years later, he said to me...well, this was in '33 I think it was..."If you ever come to New York, look me up." So I didn't have no idea...I didn't realize that he was commuting from New York to Chicago. So I went up to the room and Cow Cow says, "Sam Price!" "Hey He says, /Mayo, I got it! I taught Sam the 'Cow Cow Blues;'" said, "This little kid beat me playing the piano in Norfolk, Virginia, and I liked him, and I taught him the 'Cow Cow Blues.'" And Mayo says, "Do Come off! What'd he mean could I....? you think you can play (it)?" "Oh what do you mean, do I think I can play it?" So I played the "Cow Cow Blues" and some other things and that was the beginning of my relationship with Decca. And I recorded Peetie

Wheatstraw . As a matter of fact, I used to go... Mayo and I became inseparable and we'd go to Chicago and take like Little Brother Montgomery and find him, get him together, get his songs together and I would get his songs straightened out out in Chicago before we'd get here, so we would save time. Then we'd get a bottle of whiskey and go down the highway and end up at the Woodside Hotel. And the following day we'd go sign the contract, you know, when are you going to leave and all that business, and then I'd go in the studio with him and if they couldn't play for themselves, or if they faulted (sometimes a guy would get drunk or he would just get stage fright). George White, Peetie Wheatstraw, The Devil's Son-in-Law, The High Sheriff from Hell, Johnny Temple, Arlie Shepherd, you know, during those days, and at the same time I did a thing that Bob Crosby...da da da da da-da-da (humming)...that's "Cow Cow Blues," right? Da da da da DA da/ da-da-da-da-da-da duh. Yeah, I made an arrangement on that. It was my arrangement that I recorded. Bob Crosby took the whole arrangement, note for note, and didn't say one word to me. Well, I didn't care. You know why? Because I wasn't greedy and I was making money and I had gained recognition. I was being recognized as a piano player, although I was reluctant to, you know, to say...I knew Basie, I knew all those guys,

you know. They said I could play. But I never said I could play the piano. I never did. So, we went in and we made the "Cow Cow Blues" and after that came a sequence of things...I did "Fetch It To Me," with Don Stovall and those guys...
